newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-JAPAN AND SOUTH KOREA RAISE MORE QUESTIONS THAN ANSWERS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JAPAN AND SOUTH KOREA RAISE MORE QUESTIONS THAN ANSWERS.

text.p: FIFA said on Wednesday that the major issues surrounding the 2002 World Cup finals were agreed upon by co-hosts Japan and South Korea on Wednesday -- and then refused to say what they were.

Despite the presence of more than 20 Japanese and Korean television crews and more than 100 journalists from the print media at a news conference, FIFA vice-president and UEFA president Lennart Johansson was tight-lipped.

He declined to reveal most of the decisions taken in a three-hour meeting of the 2002 Study Group in which Japan and South Korean delegates faced each other officially for the first time since being awarded the event on May 31.

All FIFA announced publicly was that the final would be one match and not a two-legged affair, that both Japan and South Korea would qualify automatically for the finals and that 32 teams would take part in 64 matches.
An idea mooted by Japan that the finals should comprise 40 teams was rejected as was an idea from Korea that a draw should be made to decide where the final would be held.

But Johansson's silence -- and the utter refusal of any of the study group members to say anything about the meeting -- resulted in rumours flying around FIFA's headquarters with a frenzied media pack trying to hunt down any morsel of information.

Alan Rothenberg, the chief executive of the 1994 World Cup in the United States, and a technical delegate to the meeting would only say: "I am sworn to secrecy as is the rest of the committee. I have a tape over my mouth and I feel like a monk.
"I have taken a vow of silence -- though not one of celibacy. We have made recommendations today for the executive committee to endorse next month and they cannot be leaked out to the press first."
A press statement issued after the meeting said the study group had agreed to recommend six key decisions to the executive committee which meets in Barcelona on December 7.

They were the venue of the final, the name of the event, the event logo and mascot, the composition of the organising committee, the location of the main media and broadcasting centres and where the various draws for the qualifying and final rounds would be held.

FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter used the occasion to deny he had said that Japan and South Korea were moving away from one another and "were not the marriage FIFA wanted" in a recent magazine article.
"The two parties are very close but there was an embargo on them working together until they came face to face today," Blatter said. "We are all very positive and very optimistic."
What appeared odd to most media observers was the speed with which the two sides, who have reportedly been at loggerheads over most of the issues, apparently became so co-operative.

Committee member Antonio Matarrese, the former president of the Italian federation said: "One side wanted the opening ceremony more than the other, one side wanted the final more than the opening ceremony. It was a very positive and co-operative meeting."

Asked whether he was pleased about the decision on where to stage the final, Ken Naganuma, president of the Japan Football Association said: "I am neither happy nor unhappy. There are compromises that have to be made."
His Korean counterpart Dr Chung Moon-jong said: "It was a very productive meeting and we are all very happy at the outcome."
